title: About My Clerkship at Korea University
paragraphs: I did a clerkship for five weeks, from March 18 to April 19, 2024, at Korea University in Seoul, South Korea. About a month before the clerkship started, a residents' strike began across Korea, and it was unfortunate that I could hardly meet residents or local students, but the doctors guided me very kindly and carefully, so I was able to spend fulfilling days.

Korea University is one of the three major universities in Korea and has three affiliated hospitals in Korea. Anam Hospital, where I did my clerkship, introduced the da Vinci early even within Korea and is a hospital that actively works on robotic surgery. I did clerkships in breast and endocrine surgery and colorectal surgery and was able to observe many robotic operations.

For the first two weeks I did my clerkship in breast and endocrine surgery, centered on observing surgery. It was my first clerkship at Anam Hospital, and I was initially anxious about communicating in English, but I was very happy that the doctor explained each time what he was doing during surgery, and since he also answered my questions carefully, my tension eased. In particular, in the endocrine surgery clerkship, I was very impressed to observe Transoral robotic Thyroidectomy (TORT), developed by Dr. Kim, a professor at Anam Hospital. In TORT, three incisions are made inside the lower lip, a camera and robotic forceps are inserted, and the thyroid is removed from there. It is a new surgical method that makes no incision in a visible area. I could sense the devices of providing medical care that stays close to the patient, such as not only removing the lesion but making the wound inconspicuous. Also, when I told them I was interested in robotic surgery, a breast surgery doctor contacted general surgery, and I was able to observe robotic surgery for cholecystectomy for gallstones and pancreatic resection. Using a robot in these operations is rare in Japan, and I reaffirmed that in Korea robotic surgery is indicated for more diseases. In addition, the da Vinci used in the cholecystectomy was the Sp, in which the camera and forceps can be inserted through a single port, and being able to observe surgery with the Sp, of which few have been introduced in Japan, was also a valuable experience. I am truly grateful to the doctor who responded flexibly across departments.

For the following three weeks I did my clerkship in colorectal surgery, observing robot-assisted hernia surgery and laparoscopic colorectal cancer surgery and also outpatient clinics. The outpatient clinics were held in Korean, but the doctor explained each case in English, which I was very grateful for. In addition, during the colorectal surgery clerkship period, I went with the doctor to KSERS2024, a symposium on robotic surgery held in Daejeon, and to the robotic surgery center. At KSERS, through presentations and discussions I learned the characteristics of robotic surgery in the gastrointestinal and breast-endocrine fields, and at the reception I could interact with doctors from Seoul National University and doctors who had come from Japan, which became a good memory. At the robotic surgery center, I was first taught the types and history of surgical robots, and then through a simulator I learned how to operate the da Vinci, such as camera operation, arm clutch operation and suturing. For me, who am interested in robotic surgery, being allowed to actually operate the da Vinci was a truly happy experience. Until the clerkship began I was anxious about communicating in English and medical English, but as a result of being conscious of actively asking questions and going to talk to people myself, the doctors answered enthusiastically and I was able to learn a lot.

I stayed at a hotel at Dongdaemun History and Culture Park Station. I used the subway for almost all travel within Seoul, and Dongdaemun History and Culture Park Station is not only close to the university but also a station served by various lines, so it was easy for sightseeing. It was my first time living alone and going overseas alone, but public safety was good and I could live with peace of mind. Also, Korean people were truly kind, and there were many warm people who spoke up to help when I was in trouble at shops and stations. As for after the clerkship and weekends, a doctor introduced me to other exchange students, and I mostly spent time with exchange students from Singapore and Hungary. We contacted each other every day and enjoyed tourist spots in Korea, food and movies together. I was the only clerkship student from Nagoya University, and because of the residents' strike in Korea I could hardly meet local medical students, so I felt a little forlorn at times, but I could interact with other exchange students and spent every day happily.

Through this study abroad, of course I was able to learn Korean medicine, such as various robotic surgeries, but I also think I became more proactive. Being able to talk a lot and go ask questions on my own to the doctors and nurses at the clerkship site, other exchange students, and the doctors I met at KSERS, I feel, was a great growth. I think I was able to break out of my shell precisely because I placed myself in an unfamiliar environment. I express my deep gratitude to everyone at Korea University who gave me this valuable experience, and to Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. 粕谷 and everyone at the International Collaboration Office, who gave me a lot of advice. Thank you very much.
